> **▶ [Solve it on TrueInterview](https://trueinterview.io/questions/meeting-rooms-variants)** — free, no card: a runnable editor, the sample and hidden tests, a judged verdict, and the reference solution.

## Problem

This question is a family of interval-scheduling tasks. The central version supplies a list of time intervals `intervals`, each a pair (start, end). The intervals could stand for meetings, car pickup and return pairs, or server job runs. Depending on the variant, you are asked for one or more of the following:

- The smallest number of rooms, cars or servers needed so that every interval can be honored at the same time. This is the canonical minimum-meeting-rooms task, implemented as `minMeetingRooms(intervals)`.
- An assignment that says which interval goes to which room or car, so that the caller can keep a per-resource record.
- A check of whether two given intervals overlap.

The variants below are the ones that have been reported.

## Variants

**Parking-lot capacity**

Arrival and departure intervals describe cars occupying a parking lot. Using the same interval-overlap model, compute the peak number of cars present at once.

**Cyclic time (24-hour wrap)**

Intervals may wrap around midnight: an interval that ends after the day boundary continues into the next day. A follow-up asks how you would optimize if the number of intervals `N` is very large.

**Daily-recurring server jobs**

The same set of jobs runs every day. A job that cannot finish within one day is cut off at midnight and resumes the next day. One server may run several identical jobs that overlap in time, whereas different jobs need separate servers. Follow-up: a single job that spans many days needs a server of its own.

**On-call rotation consolidation**

The input is a list of on-call rotations `{name, start, end}`, using half-open intervals. Output the maximal contiguous segments during which the set of people on call stays the same. Leave out any gap in which nobody is on call. Segments are sorted by start time, and the names listed for a segment are the people active during that range.

**Gate entry and exit with priority rules**

The input is an array of `(timestamp, action)` pairs where `action` is `enter` or `exit`, and each index is a different person. For each person, return the time they actually pass through the gate, using these tie-break rules when several people want to pass at the same moment:

- If the previous tick had an enter, enter wins the tie.
- If the previous tick had an exit, exit wins the tie.
- If the previous tick had no activity, exit wins.
- Within the winning class, the lower index goes first.

An optimization is expected: rather than stepping through time one tick at a time, reach $$O(n)$$ by moving through the sorted input timestamps.

**Google Calendar free-time intersection**

The input is a set of requested attendees together with each person's busy calendar intervals. Return every time range during which all requested attendees are free.

**Car-rental assignment**

The input is a list of rental orders, each with an order ID, a pickup time and a return time. Assign every order to a car so that no two orders on the same car overlap and the number of cars is as small as possible. Return each car's full list of orders, modeling each car explicitly with its own rental record. A current version of the question instead returns a dictionary from reservation ID to assigned car ID, with a follow-up asking for the final fleet size. A return at time `t` and a pickup at time `t` may use the same car. Follow-up: if the fleet is limited to `K` cars and not every request can be served, define how the allocator detects this and how it handles the failure.

**Exact-concurrency intervals**

Compute the maximum number of meetings that are active simultaneously. Given a target concurrency `X`, also return every maximal time range in which exactly `X` meetings are active. Define the ordering of events when one meeting starts at the same timestamp that another ends; this choice decides whether a zero-width overlap is counted.

**Maximum-profit job scheduling**

Each job has a `startTime`, an `endTime` and a `profit`. Choose a set of jobs that do not overlap so that the total profit is as large as possible. This was asked as the first question of an L4 onsite round, followed in the same slot by an unrelated range-query problem.

**On-call employee metadata**

Each duty record has an employee ID, an employee name, a start time and an end time. For each time segment, return the number of employees on duty and their identifying information. This variant carries detailed complexity follow-ups: account separately for heap operations, stored employee information and output size, and explain every symbol appearing in your complexity expression.

## Examples

- Canonical minimum-meeting-rooms example: $$[[0,30],[5,10],[15,20]] \to 2$$.
- On-call consolidation: `A[10,50], B[20,60], C[30,40], D[30,40]` → `[10,20]: A`, `[20,30]: A,B`, `[30,40]: A,B,C,D`, `[40,50]: A,B`, `[50,60]: B`.
- Single-interval overlap: `intervalsOverlap([1,5],[4,7]) → true`.
- Long-running job: a 36-hour daily job cannot be handled under the cut-off-at-midnight rule, so a separate server is reserved for it.

## Interview Notes

- This family appears in Round 1 coding, Round 2 onsite coding, phone screens and as a warm-up in the FDE loop. Almost every other coding loop contains some flavor of it.
- Interviewers commonly chain two follow-ups: first, reconstruct the assignment; second, scale out to many shards or regions. The shard question invites an open-ended discussion covering per-shard processing, merging across shards and reconciliation, and the interviewer often admits the question is intentionally vague.

## Hints

<details>
<summary>Hint 1</summary>

Reduce every variant to asking how many intervals overlap at any single moment in time.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2</summary>

Sort by start time and track the earliest finishing active interval with a min-heap, or sweep over sorted start and end events.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3</summary>

Watch ties where one interval ends exactly when another begins, and keep the room assignment separate from the simple count.

</details>
